doc.title: SQL Joins
doc.objective: Write INNER and LEFT JOIN queries and predict which rows each returns when matching rows are missing.
objective_parts: Write INNER JOIN queries to combine rows from multiple tables based on a matching condition.
Write LEFT JOIN queries to include all records from the left table alongside matching right table records.
Predict which rows each JOIN type returns when matching rows are missing.

sections.title: The Missing Data Mystery
sections.body_md:
Imagine you manage a university database. One table holds student records, while another records course enrollments. When you want to see who is enrolled in what, some students seem to vanish from your reports entirely because they haven't picked a class yet, while courses without students disappear too. If you only look at one table at a time, you miss the full picture. Relational databases store data across separate, normalized tables to reduce redundancy, but to answer real questions, you need a way to stitch those tables back together based on related columns.

Quick check: before reading on, write down which rows you think a LEFT JOIN keeps.

sections.title: Combining Tables with INNER JOIN
sections.body_md:
To combine rows from two or more tables based on a shared column, you use an INNER JOIN [S4]. This operation finds the strict mathematical intersection of both datasets [S13]. It looks at a common key—such as a student ID or department ID—and returns only the rows where matching values exist in both tables [S5][S9][S15]. If a record exists in one table but has no corresponding match in the other, it is completely filtered out and excluded from your results [S4][S10].

In SQL, you specify this in your `FROM` clause [Yh4CrPHVBdE]. The syntax lists the first table, declares the `INNER JOIN` keyword alongside the second table, and uses an `ON` clause to define the matching criteria [S4][S9]. Because inner joins only output strict matches, they are highly efficient for querying tightly linked relationships, such as valid sales tied to existing products [S10][S13].

sections.title: Preserving Records with LEFT JOIN
sections.body_md:
An inner join discards unmatched rows, but what if you need to keep every single record from your primary table regardless of whether a match exists elsewhere [S10]? For this, you use a LEFT JOIN (also called a LEFT OUTER JOIN) [S3]. A left join returns all rows from the left table, paired with any matching rows from the right table [S3][S5]. 

When a row in the left table lacks a match in the right table, the query still retains that left-table row, filling in the missing right-table columns with `NULL` values [S3][S5][S11]. This makes left joins essential for auditing tasks, such as finding every customer including those who have never placed an order, or finding departments with zero staff [S11].

sections.title: Predicting Outcomes for Missing Matches
sections.body_md:
When designing queries, you must be able to predict how missing data affects your output grid. An `INNER JOIN` acts as a gatekeeper: if a foreign key is broken or missing on either side, the entire row is dropped [S4][S13]. A `LEFT JOIN` acts as an inclusive safety net for the table declared on the left side of the query, protecting its rows from deletion while padding missing right-side data with `NULL` [S3][S11].

A common pitfall occurs when placing conditions on right-table columns inside a `WHERE` clause instead of the `ON` clause [S11]. Filtering a right-table column for a non-null value in the `WHERE` clause can accidentally turn your `LEFT JOIN` back into an `INNER JOIN`, silently erasing your unmatched rows because the `WHERE` filter evaluates after the join and excludes the newly padded `NULL` values [S12].

sections.title: Working with SQL Joins
sections.body_md:
Consider two tables: `students` and `enrollments`. The `students` table has student IDs and names, while `enrollments` tracks student IDs and course IDs. Some students have not enrolled in any courses.

```python
# Simulating relational joins in Python standard library
students = [
    {"id": 1, "name": "Alice"},
    {"id": 2, "name": "Bob"},
    {"id": 3, "name": "Charlie"}
]

enrollments = [
    {"id": 1, "course": "CS101"},
    {"id": 2, "course": "CS102"}
]

# INNER JOIN simulation
inner_result = [
    (s["name"], e["course"])
    for s in students
    for e in enrollments
    if s["id"] == e["id"]
]
print("INNER:", inner_result)

# LEFT JOIN simulation
left_result = []
for s in students:
    match = [e["course"] for e in enrollments if e["id"] == s["id"]]
    if match:
        for c in match:
            left_result.append((s["name"], c))
    else:
        left_result.append((s["name"], None))
print("LEFT:", left_result)
```

```output
INNER: [('Alice', 'CS101'), ('Bob', 'CS102')]
LEFT: [('Alice', 'CS101'), ('Bob', 'CS102'), ('Charlie', None)]
```

Notice how Charlie has no course match. The inner join drops Charlie completely, whereas the left join retains Charlie and outputs `None` (SQL's `NULL`) for the course column.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions
sections.body_md:
### Misconception 1: Left joins keep rows from both tables when matches are missing
Beginners often believe a `LEFT JOIN` will preserve unmatched rows from both the left and right tables [M1]. In reality, a left join only guarantees that all rows from the *left* table are kept. Unmatched rows from the *right* table are still excluded unless you use a `FULL JOIN` [S5][S12].

### Misconception 2: Putting join filters in the WHERE clause behaves the same as the ON clause
Many learners write `LEFT JOIN` queries and filter right-table attributes in the `WHERE` clause, expecting unmatched rows to remain with nulls. Because the `WHERE` clause executes after the join is built, filtering on a right-table column can inadvertently remove your `NULL` rows, transforming your outer join into an inner join [S11].

sections.title: Query Prediction and Design Exercise
sections.body_md:
In this hands-on task, you will analyze table schemas and predict output rows.

1. Review a mock database schema containing an `employees` table (columns: `emp_id`, `name`) and a `departments` table (columns: `dept_id`, `emp_id`, `dept_name`). Note that two employees are not assigned to any department.
2. Write an `INNER JOIN` query linking `employees` and `departments` on `emp_id`. Predict how many rows will be returned if there are 5 total employees and 3 have departments [S4][S9].
3. Rewrite the query as a `LEFT JOIN` keeping `employees` on the left side [S3][S6]. Predict what values appear for the unassigned employees' department columns [S3][S5].
4. Self-check: Confirm that your inner join returns 3 rows while your left join returns all 5 rows, with `NULL` filling the missing department fields for the unassigned workers [S3][S4].

sections.title: Lesson Summary
sections.body_md:
- **INNER JOIN**: Combines rows from multiple tables based on a matching condition, returning strictly the intersecting records and dropping unmatched rows [S4][S9][S13].
- **LEFT JOIN**: Retains every record from the left table, attaching matching right-table data and placing `NULL` where matches are absent [S3][S5][S11].
- **Prediction**: Missing foreign keys cause inner joins to eliminate rows entirely, whereas left joins protect left-table rows while converting missing right-side values to `NULL` [S3][S4][S11].

quiz.question: Which SQL operation should you use when you want to retrieve every customer record from a customer table, alongside any matching orders from an orders table, ensuring customers without orders are still included?
options: CROSS JOIN
FULL JOIN
INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN
quiz.explanation: A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, paired with matching rows from the right table, and fills in NULL when there is no match.
quiz.objective_part: Write LEFT JOIN queries to include all records from the left table alongside matching right table records.
distractor_rationale: CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product and is not used for matching specific table relationships.
FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both tables, which is broader than just preserving the left table.
INNER JOIN excludes records from the left table that do not have a matching record in the right table.
correct

quiz.question: You execute an INNER JOIN between an 'authors' table and a 'books' table on 'author_id'. One author has written no books and has no matching entry in the books table. What happens to this author in the result set?
options: The author is excluded entirely from the result set.
The query throws a syntax error due to missing data.
The author is included with NULL values for book columns.
The author is duplicated for every book in the database.
quiz.explanation: An INNER JOIN acts as an intersection and gatekeeper, filtering out and completely excluding any rows that lack a matching key in both tables.
quiz.objective_part: Predict which rows each JOIN type returns when matching rows are missing.
distractor_rationale: correct
Relational databases do not throw syntax errors for missing data values during joins.
NULL values for missing matches are a feature of LEFT JOIN, not INNER JOIN.
Duplicating every book would resemble a CROSS JOIN without conditions, not an INNER JOIN.

quiz.question: How do you properly construct an INNER JOIN query in SQL to combine 'employees' and 'departments' tables based on 'department_id'?
options: SELECT * FROM employees JOIN departments MATCH employees.department_id = departments.department_id;
SELECT * FROM employees INNER JOIN departments ON employees.department_id = departments.department_id;
SELECT * FROM employees, departments USING INNER JOIN department_id;
SELECT * FROM employees INNER JOIN departments WHERE employees.department_id = departments.department_id;
quiz.explanation: Standard SQL syntax for an inner join lists the tables with the INNER JOIN keyword and specifies the matching condition using an ON clause.
quiz.objective_part: Write INNER JOIN queries to combine rows from multiple tables based on a matching condition.
distractor_rationale: The MATCH keyword is not standard SQL syntax for joining tables.
correct
The USING INNER JOIN syntax is invalid in standard SQL.
Using WHERE for join conditions is a pitfall that can alter join behavior or lead to confusion, whereas the ON clause is the correct standard construct.

quiz.question: When performing a LEFT JOIN where a row in the right table has no corresponding match in the left table, what is returned for the left table's columns in that row?
options: Default zero values
NULL values
An error code
The row is excluded from the result set
quiz.explanation: A LEFT JOIN preserves all rows from the left table; when right-table matches are missing, right-table columns are filled with NULL values.
quiz.objective_part: Predict which rows each JOIN type returns when matching rows are missing.
distractor_rationale: Databases insert NULL rather than arbitrary default zero values for unmatched columns.
correct
Missing matches in a join do not trigger error codes in SQL.
Unmatched rows from the left table are retained, not excluded.

quiz.question: Which of the following describes the key structural difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN?
options: INNER JOIN requires an ON clause, while LEFT JOIN operates without any matching condition.
INNER JOIN returns only matching intersection records, while LEFT JOIN preserves all records from the left table regardless of matches.
INNER JOIN keeps all records from both tables, while LEFT JOIN keeps only matching records.
INNER JOIN only works with numerical keys, while LEFT JOIN handles text strings.
quiz.explanation: An INNER JOIN returns only the strict intersection of matching rows, whereas a LEFT JOIN guarantees that all rows from the left table are retained.
quiz.objective_part: Predict which rows each JOIN type returns when matching rows are missing.
distractor_rationale: Both inner and left joins require a matching condition specified via an ON clause.
correct
This incorrectly reverses the operational behaviors of inner and left joins.
Both join types can handle numerical keys and text strings equally.

claims.sentence: To combine rows from two or more tables based on a shared column, you use an INNER JOIN [S4].

claims.quote: A PostgreSQL JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c15 explicitly states that a join combines rows from two or more tables based on a shared or related column.

claims.sentence: This operation finds the strict mathematical intersection of both datasets [S13].
claims.claim: An INNER JOIN operation finds the strict mathematical intersection of both datasets.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c55 explicitly describes the INNER JOIN result as a 'Strict intersection of both datasets.'

claims.sentence: It looks at a common key—such as a student ID or department ID—and returns only the rows where matching values exist in both tables [S5][S9][S15].
claims.claim: An INNER JOIN returns only the rows where matching values exist in both tables based on a common key.
claims.quote: INNER JOIN is used to retrieve rows where matching values exist in both tables.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c21 shows that an INNER JOIN returns rows where matching values exist in both tables.

claims.sentence: If a record exists in one table but has no corresponding match in the other, it is completely filtered out and excluded from your results [S4][S10].
claims.claim: Records with no corresponding match in the other table are excluded from INNER JOIN results.
claims.quote: If no match exists, the row is excluded from the result set.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c96 explicitly confirms that non-matching records are excluded from the result set.

claims.sentence: In SQL, you specify this in your `FROM` clause [Yh4CrPHVBdE].
claims.claim: SQL specifies table joins in the FROM clause.
claims.quote: The join condition of an inner join can be written either in the WHERE clause or in the JOIN clause.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c12 and other examples demonstrate specifying tables and joins within the FROM clause.

claims.sentence: The syntax lists the first table, declares the `INNER JOIN` keyword alongside the second table, and uses an `ON` clause to define the matching criteria [S4][S9].
claims.claim: SQL join syntax lists the first table, declares INNER JOIN with the second table, and uses an ON clause for matching criteria.
claims.quote: The first joined table is referenced in the FROM clause, then the LEFT JOIN is added, followed by the second table you want to join. The tables are joined on matching column values; you reference these columns in the ON clause
claims.reasoning: Evidence c81 and c50 outline the syntax order: referencing the first table, adding the join with the second table, and using an ON clause.

claims.sentence: A left join returns all rows from the left table, paired with any matching rows from the right table [S3][S5].
claims.claim: A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table paired with matching rows from the right table.
claims.quote: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c17 clearly states that a LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table alongside matching rows from the right table.

claims.sentence: When a row in the left table lacks a match in the right table, the query still retains that left-table row, filling in the missing right-table columns with `NULL` values [S3][S5][S11].
claims.claim: When a left table row lacks a match in a LEFT JOIN, missing right-table columns are filled with NULL values.
claims.quote: When a left-table row has no match on the right, the query still keeps it — and fills every right-table column with NULL instead of dropping the row.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c64 states that unmatched left rows are kept and missing right-table columns are filled with NULL.

claims.sentence: An `INNER JOIN` acts as a gatekeeper: if a foreign key is broken or missing on either side, the entire row is dropped [S4][S13].
claims.claim: An INNER JOIN drops the entire row if a foreign key is broken or missing on either side.
claims.quote: a NULL value in any one of the foreign keys can result in the entire row being eliminated from the result set, with no indication of error.
claims.reasoning: Evidence c111 explicitly states that a null or broken foreign key in an inner join causes the entire row to be eliminated.

claims.sentence: Filtering a right-table column for a non-null value in the `WHERE` clause can accidentally turn your `LEFT JOIN` back into an `INNER JOIN`, silently erasing your unmatched rows because the `WHERE` filter evaluates after the join and excludes the newly padded `NULL` values [S12].
claims.claim: Filtering a right-table column for a non-null value in the WHERE clause turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN by excluding padded NULL values.
claims.quote: Placing a condition on a right-table column in WHERE looks harmless, but NULL fails almost every comparison, so it quietly strips out the unmatched rows you were trying to keep
claims.reasoning: Evidence confirms that filtering a right-table column in the WHERE clause excludes padded NULL values, turning the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

claims.sentence: In reality, a left join only guarantees that all rows from the *left* table are kept.
claims.claim: A LEFT JOIN only guarantees that all rows from the left table are kept.
claims.quote: A LEFT JOIN changes that rule: it guarantees every row from the left table appears in the result at least once.
claims.reasoning: Evidence explicitly states that a LEFT JOIN guarantees every row from the left table is kept.

claims.sentence: Unmatched rows from the *right* table are still excluded unless you use a `FULL JOIN` [S5][S12].
claims.claim: Unmatched rows from the right table are excluded in a LEFT JOIN unless a FULL JOIN is used.
claims.quote:
- RIGHT JOIN – Returns all the data from the right table and only the matching rows from the left table. The non-matching rows’ values will be NULL.
- FULL JOIN – Returns all rows from both joined tables.
claims.reasoning: Evidence confirms unmatched rows from the right table are excluded in a LEFT JOIN and that FULL JOIN is needed to include all rows from both tables.

claims.sentence: Because the `WHERE` clause executes after the join is built, filtering on a right-table column can inadvertently remove your `NULL` rows, transforming your outer join into an inner join [S11].
claims.claim: The WHERE clause executes after the join is built.
claims.quote: - WHERE — filters are applied to the joined result, including those NULL-padded rows.
claims.reasoning: Evidence states that the WHERE clause executes after the join is built.

claims.sentence: INNER JOIN: Combines rows from multiple tables based on a matching condition, returning strictly the intersecting records and dropping unmatched rows [S4][S9][S13].
claims.claim: An INNER JOIN returns strictly intersecting records and drops unmatched rows.
claims.quote: | INNER JOIN | Strict intersection of both datasets. | Completely Excluded. | Completely Excluded. |
claims.reasoning: Evidence confirms that an INNER JOIN returns the strict intersection and completely excludes unmatched rows.

claims.sentence: LEFT JOIN: Retains every record from the left table, attaching matching right-table data and placing `NULL` where matches are absent [S3][S5][S11].
claims.claim: A LEFT JOIN retains every record from the left table and places NULL where matches are absent.
claims.quote: A LEFT JOIN (also written LEFT OUTER JOIN) returns every row from the "left" table in your query, plus the matching row(s) from the "right" table. When a left-table row has no match on the right, the query still keeps it — and fills every right-table column with NULL
claims.reasoning: Evidence confirms that a LEFT JOIN retains every record from the left table and places NULL where matches are absent.

confusions.quote: When performing a LEFT JOIN where a row in the right table has no corresponding match in the left table, what is returned for the left table's columns in that row?
confusions.why: This is a trick question or a conceptual confusion because a left join by definition always preserves the left table, so rows in the left table are never missing when matched against the right table; rather, it is the right table rows that are missing.
